Lecture 1: Introduction and Scope

Description: In this lecture, Prof. Winston introduces artificial intelligence and provides a brief history of the field. The last ten minutes are devoted to information about the course at MIT.

      26:48that an arch is something that has to have the flat part on
      26:51top, and the two sides can't touch, and the top may or may

      26:59In the late dawn age, though, the most important thing,
      27:01perhaps, was what you look at with me on Wednesday next.

      27:09And a program was written at Stanford that did diagnosis of
      27:14bacterial infections of the blood.
      27:16It turned out to do it better than most doctors, most
      27:21general practitioners.
      27:22It was never used, curiously enough.
      27:26Because nobody cares what your problem actually is.
      27:31They just give you a broad spectrum antibiotic that'll
      27:33kill everything.
      27:36But this late dawn age system, the so-called [INAUDIBLE]
      27:39system, was the system that launched a thousand companies,
      27:46because people started building expert systems built
      27:48on that technology.
      27:50Here's that you don't know you used, or that was

      27:53If you go through, for example, the Atlanta airport,

      28:59But nevertheless, Deep Blue, by processing data like a
      29:04bulldozer processes gravel, was able to

      29:11So what's the right way?
      29:13That's the age we're in right now.
      29:15I will of course be inducing programs for those ages as we

      29:19There is a question of what age we're in right now.
      29:22And it's always dangerous to name an age when

      32:35So now we have to think about why we ought to be optimistic

      33:12be that way.
      33:14The high school idea is that we evolved through slow,
      33:19gradual, and continuous improvement.
      33:23But that doesn't seem to be the way it happened.
      33:25There are some characteristics of our species that are

      33:45years in our present anatomical form.

      34:00but other than that--
      34:03probably naked, too--
      34:05other than that, you wouldn't be able to tell the
      34:08difference, especially at MIT.
      34:15And so the ensuing 150,000 years was a period in which we
      34:21humans didn't actually amount to much.
      34:25But somehow, shortly before 50,000 years ago, some small
      34:30group of us developed a capability that separated us
      34:34from all other species.
      34:37It was an accident of evolution.
      34:40And these accidents may or may not happen, but it happened to

      34:45It's also the case that we probably necked down as a

      35:12And that conclusion is--
      35:15I'll quote Chomsky.
      35:16He's the voice of authority.
      35:18"It seems that shortly before 50,000 years ago, some small
      35:22group of us acquired the ability to take two concepts,
      35:26and combine them to make a third concept, without
      35:29disturbing the original two concepts, without limit." And
      35:33from a perspective of an AI person like me, what Chomsky
      35:37seems to be saying is, we learned how to begin to
      35:39describe things, in a way that was intimately
      35:42connected with language.
      35:43And that, in the end, is what separates us from the
      35:46chimpanzees.
      35:49So you might say, well let's just study language.

      35:53So language does two things.

      35:57Descriptions enable us to tell stories.
      36:00And storytelling and story understanding is what all of

      36:03That's going up.
      36:04And going down enables us to marshal the resources of our

      36:12to imagine things we've never seen.

      36:20Imagine running down the street with a

      36:29The water sloshes out.

      36:43There was internal imagination simulation.
